title: The Box on the Sandbar: Motomachi's Forts, Fires and Foreign Consuls
standfirst: A tombolo joining an island hill to the mainland, a box-shaped fort that gave the town its name, and a history of fire so relentless that the government once rewrote the street plan to stop it: this dossier follows Motomachi from a fifteenth-century stockade to the stone and brick townscape a visitor walks through today.

sections.heading: A Fort Shaped Like a Box

paragraphs.text: Hakodate's 1911 district history describes the town's ground as shaped like a gourd: a narrow, pinched sandbar in the middle, with the isolated hill of Mount Hakodate holding up the southern end and the flat Kameda plain opening out to the north. The Ainu name for the site was Usukeshi, which the same history explains as a corruption of Ushorokeshi, "the tip of the bay" — the same root, it notes, that gives the Iburi town of Usu its name. Mount Hakodate itself, an isolated andesite hill worn into the long, low silhouette of a lying-down ox, supplied the stone for Goryōkaku's walls and much else besides; from 1897 the whole mountain was closed to civilians and turned over to army coastal artillery, which reshaped its summit with gun emplacements.

The town's own name is older than any of that. In 1454, according to both the city's own historical summary and a local museum register of cultural properties, a warrior named Kōno Masamichi arrived from Tsugaru and built a fortified residence at Usukeshi, roughly 63 metres by 50 metres, ringed with earthen banks and dry moats. Because it was shaped like a box, people called it Hakodate — "box fort" — and wrote it 箱館. The site, in today's Yayoi-chō, stayed in continuous administrative use for four centuries: the Kameda magistrate's office moved there in 1741, the shogunate's own Hakodate magistracy in 1802. Only in 1869, when Ezo became Hokkaido, did the government swap the character 箱 for the similarly pronounced 函, giving the modern spelling 函館.

sections.heading: Guns on the Beach, Bells on the Hill

paragraphs.text: Matsumae-domain and shogunate control of the area brought its own anxieties, not least a Russian navy that had been probing the Kuril Islands and the Ezo coast since the early 1800s; in 1811 Japanese forces at Kunashiri seized the Russian surveying-ship captain Vasily Golovnin, and in the tangled hostage exchange that followed, the Hakodate merchant Takadaya Kahei was himself briefly seized and taken to Kamchatka before the two sides negotiated a settlement. By the 1850s it was American rather than Russian ships that worried the authorities: a surviving town proclamation, issued when a US squadron was expected off Hakodate, ordered women, children and anyone under thirteen out of the waterfront district into the hills, banned selling liquor to sailors on the grounds that "drink makes them violent," forbade townspeople from peering at the foreigners through shutters or chimneys, and told merchants to accept small gifts rather than risk giving offence.

Hakodate opened to foreign trade in 1859, one of the first ports Japan opened under its new commercial treaties, and consulates followed within the year. Russia's was among the first: its consul secured a plot on the hillside, and in 1860 a chapel was built there as the consulate's annex. A young priest named Nicholas arrived the following year as that chapel's chaplain; working from this hillside base he became the first missionary to establish Orthodox Christianity in Japan, before moving to Tokyo in 1872 to build a national church. The chapel he served in was rebuilt after fire in 1916 as the Church of the Resurrection that still stands on the hill, its bell — known locally as "Gan-gan-dera" — still ringing over Motomachi.

sections.heading: A Town That Kept Catching Fire

paragraphs.text: No account of Hakodate can avoid fire. A tally kept in the 1935 city history counts twenty-two fires of a hundred houses or more between 1873 and 1921 alone — one every two years and five months on average, and in the worst stretch, from 1907 to 1921, one every twenty months. One entry stands out for how it ties disaster to war: on 11 May 1869, fugitive shogunate soldiers under Enomoto Takeaki, cornered in the last weeks of the Boshin War, set fire to a lumberyard near Benten-chō, and the "fugitives' fire" burned 872 households. Ten years later, on the night of 6 December 1879, a fire from Horie-chō burned through thirty-three neighbourhoods and 2,326 households, including thirty-one public buildings; the 1935 history calls it "unprecedented" and says the city seemed for a time to have simply vanished.

That 1879 fire is why Motomachi looks the way it does. The Colonization Commission's director, Kuroda Kiyotaka, personally ordered the street plan redrawn: the main thoroughfare was widened from roughly four ken to thirteen (about 24 metres), side streets to at least six ken, all laid dead straight, and — the crucial rule — buildings along the main street and along every road running from the hillside down to the shore had to be built of stone, brick or plastered earthen-walled dozō construction, fireproof by design. Loans subsidised those who could not afford it, the Yachigashira wetland was reclaimed as relocation land, and new quarries were opened on the mountain's back slope to supply the stone. The stone and brick streetscape visitors now photograph in Motomachi is, in large part, a disaster-recovery regulation made permanent.

sections.heading: War's Last Stand and a Prefecture's Capital

paragraphs.text: The Boshin War itself ended a few kilometres north of this district, at the star-shaped fort of Goryōkaku, where Enomoto's holdout government surrendered on 18 May 1869 after the flagship Kaiten was defeated in the bay. The victors had little patience for the fort afterward: the War Ministry took it over, and by 1871 most of its buildings had been dismantled, their timber shipped off to help build the new capital of Sapporo. Soldiers drilled on the empty grounds from 1873 to 1897, before the city was given the site in 1913 and opened it as a public park the following year; it is now protected as Japan's only special historic site north of Honshu.

Hakodate's own administrative rank rose and fell with the fire's smoke barely cleared. When the Colonization Commission was abolished in 1882 and its territory split into three prefectures, Hakodate became a prefectural capital in its own right — though, the city's 1935 history notes dryly, the wounds of the 1879 fire were still unhealed and trade was in a general slump when the change took effect. Emperor Meiji had already toured the town the previous year, in 1881, inspecting its courthouse, customs house and shipyard; the prefecture itself lasted only until 1886, when the government folded Hakodate, Sapporo and Nemuro back together under a single Hokkaido Agency based in Sapporo, leaving Hakodate a sub-prefectural office instead.

sections.heading: The Second Fire and a New Public Hall

paragraphs.text: Fireproofing rules or not, Hakodate burned again. On the night of 25–26 August 1907 a fire that began in a soap factory on Higashikawa-chō, driven by a strong east wind, burned some 12,390 households according to the 1935 city history — by the account of the Kanemori warehouse company itself, nearly two-thirds of the town — destroying the British and Russian consulates, several schools, the prefectural sub-office and the town's own meeting hall along with it.

Two of the district's best-known landmarks rose directly from that fire's ashes. The merchant Watanabe Kumashirō, whose warehouse company had lost six buildings, ordered fireproof reconstruction at once; the new brick warehouses were finished in May 1909 and are the Kanemori Red Brick Warehouse that stands on the waterfront today. A few streets up the hill, the destroyed town hall and chamber of commerce were replaced by a new public hall: local fundraising fell short of the cost, so the merchant Sōma Teppei personally donated 50,000 of the roughly 58,000 yen needed, and the building — designed by the ward's own engineer, Konishi Asajirō — was completed in September 1910. It has been a nationally designated Important Cultural Property since 1974.

The worst fire came in 1934, and it began with weather rather than carelessness. From early afternoon a storm off the Tsugaru Strait blew ever harder; by the time flames broke out at 6:50 p.m. in a private house in Sumiyoshi-chō, gusts were already tearing roofs off buildings across the city, and the fire chief, Katsuta Yakichi, later broadcast that he himself was thrown against a utility pole by the wind and knocked down three or four times while trying to direct his crews. Six successive firebreak lines were set across the town's basin-shaped streets and broken one after another as the gale, gusting past 30 metres a second, carried burning debris ahead of the flames; Katsuta's own order to his division chiefs, to fight on independently if they lost contact with each other, closed with words he meant as a possible farewell: "do your best." The fire was not brought fully under control until roughly six the next morning.

The City of Hakodate's own figure for the dead is 2,166 — a toll in which burning was not even the largest cause: the city's breakdown records 748 deaths by fire, 217 by exposure to cold, 143 by suffocation, and 917 by drowning, as people fleeing the flames went into the harbour and the sea in the cold of a Hokkaido March and could not get out again. Roughly 102,000 people, close to two-thirds of the city's population, were left without homes, and more than eleven thousand buildings burned across twenty-two fully destroyed neighbourhoods and eighteen more partly burned; a social-welfare association's own disaster record, compiled within three years of the fire, gives closely matching figures for both the households affected and the pattern of deaths.

sections.heading: Ferry's End, Preservation, and Reading the Ground Today

paragraphs.text: Hakodate's other great transformation came from the sea. For decades the Seikan ferries were the only way to move a train, a truck or a family between Honshu and Hokkaido; that service ended on 13 March 1988, the year the Seikan Tunnel opened beneath the strait instead. One of the last ferries, the Mashū-maru, is still moored at its original berth as a memorial ship, its bridge and radio room kept as they were on the final crossing.

In the very same year, 1988, the city designated the hillside and waterfront around this dossier's study area — Yayoi-chō, Ō-chō, Suehiro-chō, Motomachi and part of Toyokawa-chō, about 14.5 hectares along a roughly 1.5-kilometre route from the harbour up to Motomachi Park — a traditional buildings preservation district; national recognition followed in 1989. Walk it today and the layers described above are still legible within a few hundred metres of each other: the fireproof stone and brick built under Kuroda's 1880s building code, the Orthodox church rebuilt after the 1907 fire, the Old Public Hall raised with Sōma Teppei's money the same decade, and, on the quiet slope of Yayoi-chō, the flat ground where Kōno Masamichi's box-shaped fort gave the whole city its name in 1454.

timeline.what: Kōno Masamichi builds a box-shaped fort at Usukeshi; the settlement becomes known as Hakodate.
The Golovnin incident: Russian and Japanese hostage-taking around Kunashiri draws in the Hakodate merchant Takadaya Kahei.
Town proclamations order residents to evacuate women and children and avoid provoking foreign crews when American ships are expected.
Hakodate opens to foreign trade; consulates, including Russia's, follow within the year.
Fugitive shogunate troops set the "fugitives' fire," burning 872 households, weeks before their final defeat.
Enomoto Takeaki surrenders Goryōkaku, ending the Boshin War; the fort is later stripped for timber sent to Sapporo.
Ezo is renamed Hokkaido and the town's name is respelled 函館.
A fire burns 2,326 households; the Colonization Commission responds by mandating fireproof stone-and-brick construction on the main streets.
Hakodate is briefly the seat of its own prefecture before Hokkaido's administration is recentralised in Sapporo.
Fire burns roughly two-thirds of the city, including both consulates and the town hall.
The Kanemori warehouses are rebuilt in fireproof brick and the new Public Hall, funded largely by Sōma Teppei, is completed.
A wind-driven fire kills 2,166 people by the city's own count, most of them by drowning.
The Seikan ferry service ends; the same year the Motomachi–Suehiro-chō preservation district is designated.

walk.name: Motomachi–Suehiro-chō Traditional Buildings Preservation District
walk.ja: 元町末広町伝統的建造物群保存地区
walk.what: Follow the roughly 1.5 km route from the harbour up to Motomachi Park; nationally protected since 1989, it holds most of the sites below within a few streets of one another.

walk.name: Hakodate Orthodox Church, Church of the Resurrection
walk.ja: 函館ハリストス正教会（復活聖堂）
walk.what: Rebuilt in 1916 on the site of the Russian consulate's 1860 chapel, where the priest Nicholas began Japan's first Orthodox mission in 1861; listen for the bell known locally as "Gan-gan-dera".

walk.name: Kanemori Red Brick Warehouse
walk.what: Fireproof brick warehouses rebuilt in 1909 after the 1907 fire destroyed their wooden predecessors; still standing on the waterfront they were built to protect.

walk.name: Old Public Hall of Hakodate Ward
walk.what: A Western-style hall of 1910, largely paid for by the merchant Sōma Teppei after the 1907 fire destroyed the previous meeting hall; a National Important Cultural Property since 1974.

walk.name: Site of Usukeshi Kōno-tate, Yayoi-chō
walk.ja: 宇須岸河野館跡（弥生町）
walk.what: The flat ground in today's Yayoi-chō where Kōno Masamichi's box-shaped fort stood from 1454, giving the city its name; later magistrates' offices occupied the same site for centuries.

walk.name: Old British Consulate (Kaikō Memorial Museum)
walk.ja: 函館市旧イギリス領事館（開港記念館）
walk.what: A former consulate building, now a city-run museum recalling the era of Commodore Perry's calls and the port's opening to foreign trade.

deepResearchLeads.what: Household-by-household or lot-by-lot records of who rebuilt what after the 1879 and 1907 fires, and how the fireproof-construction loans were actually used
deepResearchLeads.where: Hakodate City Central Library's local-history division and the Hokkaido Prefectural Archives (北海道立文書館)
deepResearchLeads.how: Request the library's local-history reference desk for post-fire reconstruction ledgers and old land registers (旧土地台帳) by lot number.

deepResearchLeads.what: Foreign consular correspondence on the 1907 and 1934 fires (each of which damaged or destroyed consulate buildings) and on daily life in the foreign settlement
deepResearchLeads.where: UK National Archives (FO series, Hakodate consulate), US National Archives, and Russian diplomatic archives for the 1860s Russian consulate
deepResearchLeads.how: Search the UK National Archives' Discovery catalogue under Foreign Office correspondence for Hakodate; equivalent searches for US State Department consular despatches.

deepResearchLeads.what: A fuller, victim-by-victim account of the 21 March 1934 fire, beyond the aggregate statistics used here
deepResearchLeads.where: The Hakodate Fire Department's own archive and the Hakodate Central Library's newspaper morgue (函館日日新聞, 函館毎日新聞, spring 1934)
deepResearchLeads.how: Request the fire department's historical records section and the library's microfilm reading room for the relevant weeks of both newspapers.

deepResearchLeads.what: Archaeological findings from the Usukeshi Kōno-tate site and other 15th-16th century Wajin-Ainu contact sites beneath today's Motomachi
deepResearchLeads.where: Hakodate City's buried-cultural-property division and the Hakodate City Museum
deepResearchLeads.how: Request published excavation reports (発掘調査報告書) for Yayoi-cho and neighbouring blocks.

deepResearchLeads.what: Records of the Seikan ferry's wartime and postwar operations, including the 1954 Toya Maru sinking's effect on Hakodate itself
deepResearchLeads.where: JR Hokkaido's corporate archive and the Mashū-maru memorial museum's own collection
deepResearchLeads.how: Contact the museum directly, and JR Hokkaido's public relations or archives office for company-history materials.

caveats: Household and casualty figures for the 1907 and 1934 fires vary slightly between the sources used here (the 1935 city history's 1934 death count of 2,165 versus the city's current official figure of 2,166, for instance); this dossier follows the city's own current figure where the two differ and names the 1935 source separately.

This dossier could not confirm the Old British Consulate building's construction year, the date it stopped serving as a consulate, or its cultural-property designation date from any source opened in this session, and so states none of them; a fact-checker with access to the museum's own historical panels could add them.

Two internet-accessible NDL items likely to be useful — a c.1899 town history and a 1902 guidebook — returned server errors from the NDL Lab API on every attempt in this session and so were not read; they are listed in furtherReading instead.
The 1454 founding date and the fort's dimensions rest on the city's own summary and a regional cultural-property register rather than on an NDL source read directly in this session.
